plan.angle: Title: 'Is Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Linked to Less Diabetic Eye Disease? #shorts'. Opening line by 10 s: 'A large health-records study linked tirzepatide to lower rates of diabetic eye disease over 12 months, vs lifestyle changes alone. Linked to, not proof.' On screen: 'adults with diabetes + overweight/obesity · 173,846 matched patients · 12 months · observational · Ophthalmology 2026'. Give absolute rates per arm from the paper. One line defining retinopathy. One calm line: 'Big, fast drops in blood sugar can briefly worsen retinopathy in some people, so if you already have it, tell your eye doctor and prescriber.' Action: keep regular diabetic eye exams. Brief GI side-effects line. Then 'Don't stop or change your current medicines on your own' and the prescriber line. No emoji.
plan.working_title: Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Protect Your Eyes in Diabetes? #shorts
plan.why: Fits our winning formula: a named drug, a 'what does it do to my body?' question and a practical action. Few creators cover it and it's framed as a benefit. Safety-scare framing underperforms for us, so we avoid it here. | fact-check: Verified: 'Tirzepatide and Reduced Risk of Diabetic Retinopathy and Related Complications: A Multicenter US Cohort Study', Ophthalmology 2026 (PubMed 41577258). Retrospective TriNetX cohort, propensity-matched, 173,846 patients (86,923 per arm). Adults with diabetes and overweight/obesity, vs lifestyle intervention alone with no exposure to weight-loss drugs. 12-month outcomes: incident or progressive DR and interventions (anti-VEGF, PRP). Issues: (1) the working title 'Protect Your Eyes' is causal and too reassuring for an observational study. Use 'linked to'. (2) State the 12-month window and that the comparator is a coded 'lifestyle intervention' group. Residual confounding is possible (people prescribed tirzepatide may differ in access and care). (3) Absolute risks per group must come from the paper's own table, not press coverage. If absolute rates aren't available, give no relative figure. (4) Be balanced. Fast drops in blood sugar have been linked to early worsening of retinopathy in some people, and a real-world cohort has examined early worsening on tirzepatide (PMC12361273). One calm line supports the eye-exam action, especially for people who already have retinopathy. That fits better than NAION. Leave NAION out. (5) Don't claim the drug works for eyes via weight or sugar unless the paper says so.

package.title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) linked to less diabetic eye disease? #shorts
package.description:
A large health-records study (n=173,846) linked tirzepatide to lower rates of diabetic retinopathy over 12 months vs a group coded as lifestyle changes alone — linked to, not proof it caused it. If you already have retinopathy: in type 2 diabetes, a fast improvement in blood sugar has been linked to a temporary worsening, so tell your eye doctor and prescriber, and keep your eye exams at least once a year or as your eye doctor advises.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Don't stop or change your current medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Tirzepatide and Reduced Risk of Diabetic Retinopathy and Related Complications: A Multicenter US Cohort Study — Ophthalmology (2026) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41577258/
2. MOUNJARO (tirzepatide) Full Prescribing Information — Eli Lilly and Company / U.S. FDA (current revision, accessed Oct 2026) https://pi.lilly.com/us/mounjaro-uspi.pdf
3. Diabetic Retinopathy — National Eye Institute (NIH), last reviewed Sep 11, 2025 https://www.nei.nih.gov/learn-about-eye-health/eye-conditions-and-diseases/diabetic-retinopathy

social.instagram_caption:
A 2026 study in people with diabetes and overweight or obesity links tirzepatide (Mounjaro) to lower rates of diabetic eye disease — but "linked to" isn't "proof it causes it."

What the study found:
🔹 173,846 matched patients (86,923 per group), tracked over 12 months
🔹 Lower rates of diabetic retinopathy vs a group coded as lifestyle changes alone
🔹 Diabetic retinopathy = damage to the blood vessels in the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye

The catch: it's observational. People prescribed tirzepatide may differ in access to care, so this can't prove the drug caused the lower rates.

One calm heads-up: in type 2 diabetes, a fast improvement in blood sugar has been linked to a temporary worsening of retinopathy. If you already have it, tell your eye doctor and prescriber.

The practical move: keep your regular diabetic eye exams, at least once a year or as your eye doctor advises. Common side effects are mostly gut-related, like nausea and diarrhea.

Save this for your next eye exam, and share it with someone on tirzepatide.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Don't stop or change your current medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe, so it passes. The three minor wording fixes below are optional; making them would match the sources more closely.

What I checked:
- **The study (src1) is real.** The title matches, and it was published in Ophthalmology on Jan 21, 2026 (Shah et al., Weill Cornell). It's a retrospective TriNetX cohort of 173,846 propensity-matched adults with diabetes plus overweight or obesity (86,923 per group). It compares tirzepatide with lifestyle intervention alone over 12 months.
- **The study's wording supports ours.** It says tirzepatide was "associated with" lower rates of new or worsening retinopathy and fewer complications. So "linked to, not proof" and the observational caveat in s4 are correct.
- **The eye-health page (src3, NEI) supports s3 and s6.** It defines retinopathy as affecting the blood vessels in the retina, "the light-sensitive layer of tissue in the back of your eye". It recommends a dilated eye exam "at least once a year" for people with diabetes (last reviewed Sep 11, 2025).
- **The Mounjaro US label (src2) supports s5 and s7.** It carries the warning that rapid improvement in glucose control has been associated with temporary worsening of retinopathy, and that patients with a history of retinopathy should be monitored. The common side effects are mostly gut-related.

Safety: the prescriber line, "don't stop or change your medicines", the side effects and the existing-retinopathy caveat are all there. There's no dosing advice. The script answers the question in s2, about 8 s in.

issues.claim: big, fast drops in blood sugar can briefly worsen retinopathy in some people
issues.problem: The label's wording is more careful: rapid improvement in glucose control 'has been associated with' a temporary worsening, and the warning applies to people with type 2 diabetes. 'Can briefly worsen' sounds a little more causal than the label.
issues.fix: One calm heads-up: in type 2 diabetes, a fast improvement in blood sugar has been linked to a temporary worsening of retinopathy. So if you already have it, tell your eye doctor and prescriber.

issues.problem: 173,846 is both groups added together. A viewer could read it as 173,846 people on tirzepatide. Our rule is to label group sizes.
issues.fix: stat_label: "matched adults (86,923 per group), diabetes plus overweight/obesity"

audio.soundNotes: Music already sits well inside the target window (−13.5 dB under voice, −13.8 dB in pauses), so only kept it at unity gain. Thinned two redundant SFX clusters (duplicate ticks layered exactly under other cues, and a 6-hit swoosh/pop pileup at 24.5–25.0s down to 3), pulled down two cues that spiked to about −6 to −8 dB under the voice during speech (i36, i44) to the −14/−20 dB felt zone, and nudged up the closing swell/whoosh (i66/67) slightly so the final "ask your prescriber" CTA lands with a touch more presence. Added three bespoke accents (shutter click on the retinopathy label, a restrained dark sting on the "catch" turn, and a warm closing chime) to sell key story beats without competing with narration.
